lines.text: force. Prayerful waiting upon God bears fruit in man's inner
detachment and freedom, with the kindness and honesty
which flow from it; in man's peaceableness of disposition
and readiness to suffer for the good. And now conversely it
should be said that all this is only possible on the basis of
genuine trust. These fruits of the spirit are not something
deliberately cultivated or forced, they grow naturally in the
soul of the man whose life is rooted in his trustful waiting on
God.
HII
The one who waits! Thus may we characterize in general
terms the life of the Christian; the description fits him just
as does that which qualifies him as the viator, the pilgrim.
In this connexion the thought of Jung-Stilling occurs to our
minds: "Blessed are the homesick; for they shall return to
their homes!" The Christian is essentially a pilgrim who is
engaged in a journey, who has turned his back on the old
world and is directing his steps to the future which God will
create. And for the same reason we may describe him as the
one who waits.
But is not this attitude characteristic of all men as such?
Is not every man at heart filled with discontent about the
present and expectation of the future? Is it not part of man's
essential being never to be able to say to the present moment:
"Tarry, I pray, thou art so beautiful!" Is it not essentially
human to be ever occupied with a tense expectation of the
coming moment that shall bring us satisfaction? No doubt
we often deceive ourselves about this, and many a time it
may seem to us that we experience a moment of fulfilment
to which we would like to hold fast. But if such a feeling does
not rest simply on the suppression and temporary oblivion of
our cares, which will soon assail us again, then in a really
fulfilled moment it is only apparently so. For such a moment
always contains the promise of a future, and fills us precisely
with tense expectancy.
